parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a written incident report within 10 days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk to their model, and promptly provide material updates and protective instructions.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a written incident report within 10 days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk to their model, and promptly provide material updates and protective instructions.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a written incident report within 10 days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk to their model, and promptly provide material updates and protective instructions. Manufacturers must keep incident records and submit an annual model-level incident summary to regulators; they must not omit incidents because the cause is uncertain.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Manufacturers must submit model-specific results, sample sizes, and corrective-action plans to the relevant regulator, and disclose the model's test results and failure rate to customers who buy that model. A failure rate above 5% requires a corrective-action plan and follow-up test within 90 days; it does not by itself bar sale.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit model-specific results, sample sizes, and corrective-action plans to the relevant regulator, and disclose the model’s test results and failure rate to customers who buy that model. A failure rate above 5% requires a corrective-action plan and follow-up test within 90 days; it does not by itself bar sale. Regulators may require additional safeguards where results or field incidents indicate a safety risk. Review the threshold against field and test data after two years.

parameters.quote: New units manufactured 24 months or more after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off option. For already-installed units, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent risk-control plan within 6 years of adoption, prioritizing models or locations presenting the greatest risk. Where remote shut-off cannot be safely retrofitted, the manufacturer must provide an alternative mitigation and notify affected customers.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units manufactured 24 months or more after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off option. For already-installed units, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent risk-control plan within 6 years of adoption, prioritizing models or locations presenting the greatest risk. Where remote shut-off cannot be safely retrofitted, the manufacturer must provide an alternative mitigation and notify affected customers.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units manufactured 24 months or more after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off option. For already-installed units, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent risk-control plan within 6 years of adoption, prioritizing models or locations presenting the greatest risk. Where remote shut-off cannot be safely retrofitted, the manufacturer must provide an alternative mitigation and notify affected customers. Regulators may require earlier action for a specific model presenting an imminent risk.

parameters.quote: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression meeting regulator-approved performance and maintenance requirements. Before that date, manufacturers must assess fire risk for each model and document the mitigation measures used.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression meeting regulator-approved performance and maintenance requirements. Before that date, manufacturers must assess fire risk for each model and document the mitigation measures used.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression meeting regulator-approved performance and maintenance requirements. Before that date, manufacturers must assess fire risk for each model and document the mitigation measures used. Regulators may require earlier model-specific safeguards where evidence indicates an imminent or unacceptable risk.

parameters.quote: Regulators must assess the validated rate and other evidence and determine proportionate protective action, which may include a recall. A recall is required when regulators determine that the model presents an imminent serious risk and no equally protective measure is available.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: Regulators must assess the validated rate and other evidence and determine proportionate protective action, which may include a recall. A recall is required when regulators determine that the model presents an imminent serious risk and no equally protective measure is available.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase, customers must receive clear safety information for the model, including safety instructions, material incident trends, the model’s per-model 55 °C test results and failure rate, and any applicable corrective actions. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of material new risks and provide protective actions and updates. If a model’s annual thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000 installed units, the manufacturer must promptly notify regulators, investigate and validate the rate, and submit a corrective-action plan. Regulators must assess the validated rate and other evidence and determine proportionate protective action, which may include a recall. A recall is required when regulators determine that the model presents an imminent serious risk and no equally protective measure is available.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
ground_truth_claims.message_text: Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year. Company-wide, Northwind recorded 8.6 thermal incidents per 100,000 units. These figures support sharing model-specific results with regulators and using corrective actions and follow-up testing for exceedances; a fixed 5% limit that automatically bars a model from sale would have a material impact. Per-model failure rates should not be published to the general public.

judge_section_notes: The final text keeps Northwind's red lines: S2 has no sales stop at 5% and no public publication of per-model rates, and S3 sets a 6-year retrofit deadline. Halcyon's red lines are met through per-model results going to purchasers in S2 and S5, and a 36-month built-in suppression deadline in S4. S1 (24-hour reporting, all incidents) is the strongest and most protective section for both companies, while S5 leaves recall to regulator discretion with no numeric mandatory trigger, and S3 sets new-unit shut-off at 24 months.
